Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the lexical idea remains straightforward: rain came down.

This Hebrew word means “poor,” describing someone or something in a low, diminished, or needy condition. It appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including descriptions of poor people and language expressing weakness or decline. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a condition of lacking strength, resources, or standing.

Zattu is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Zattu” in the English versions represented here. It does not function as a general word describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept; rather, it serves as a proper name in the biblical record. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the land. This name is connected with Joshua’s account of conquered territory and its later designation among the lands given to Israel.

“Hazar” is a place name in the Hebrew Old Testament, referring to a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Harnepher is a personal name, rendered “Harnepher” in the Bible. It refers to an individual named in the Old Testament, rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:14, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. This Hebrew word is a personal name: Tob-adonijah. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The available record gives no separate short definition or approved alternate meaning, so the safest explanation is its naming function. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament data, with both occurrences in 2 Chronicles 17:8. Its precise role there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, not to the name by itself.

This Hebrew word means “afraid,” describing a person who is afraid in relation to a threatening situation. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Jeremiah, so it is rare in this corpus rather than a word used broadly across the Old Testament. This Hebrew word means “shut.” It describes an action that prevents something from continuing, proceeding, or remaining open. It can describe restraining water, stopping people from giving, preventing someone from speaking or acting, or closing something. The approved renderings suggest that it can add emphasis or help express ability in context.

Abimael is a personal name preserved in English as “Abimael.” It identifies an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice, in Genesis 10:28 and 1 Chronicles 1:22. Its role is not defined by the name itself; the surrounding biblical passages determine the person’s place and significance. This is a proper name, not a general word describing something.

This Hebrew word refers to a “feast,” a special occasion centered on a shared meal. It functions as a noun naming the event itself rather than an action or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 5:1. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s basic sense identifies a celebratory meal or banquet.

This Hebrew noun refers to a barn, a place used for storing harvested grain. Its clearest ordinary meaning is therefore a storage building associated with agricultural produce. The word occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus represented here, including one occurrence in Haggai and one in Isaiah. Its precise role in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central lexical idea is a barn or grain-storage place.

It functions as the thing acted upon in many passages, such as making, eating, or remembering it. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word refers to decorative coverings or tapestry—textile furnishings used as part of an interior setting. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Proverbs, and is rendered “coverings” and “tapestry.” The central idea is a woven or spread textile that provides beauty, covering, or adornment within a room. Its precise force in either proverb depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself points to finished fabric furnishings rather than a person, action, or abstract quality.

Meremoth is a personal name, referring to a man rather than expressing a general word or idea. It appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra and Nehemiah, and is consistently rendered “Meremoth.” The name occurs in lists and records involving priests, families, and work connected with Jerusalem’s restoration. Since the available passages identify the person by name but do not provide a definition of the name itself, its ordinary meaning here is its designation of this individual. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means “sweet.” It describes something as having sweetness or becoming sweet, depending on how it functions in the sentence. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, appearing in Exodus, Job, Psalms, and Proverbs. Its basic sense remains focused on sweetness, while the surrounding verse determines what is described as sweet. This word is found in Exodus 15:25, Job 20:12, Job 21:33, Psalm 55:14, and Proverbs 9:17.

This Hebrew word describes something as hollow or empty. It is used of physical objects with an open interior, such as parts of the tabernacle and temple furnishings. It also appears in Job in a figurative expression connected with emptiness or vanity. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its meaning is fairly focused rather than broad. In English translations, it is chiefly rendered “hollow,” while “was” may appear as part of the surrounding sentence rather than as the word’s central meaning.

Its central idea remains a plague: an affliction recognized as significant and requiring attention within the scriptural setting.

This Hebrew verb means “draw,” expressing an action performed on something or someone. It is used five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once in 2 Samuel and four times in Jeremiah. The word functions as an action word rather than a name or description, so its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence. Its repeated use in Jeremiah shows that this action can be expressed in more than one setting, while retaining the central idea of drawing.

This Hebrew verb means “come,” describing movement toward a place or arrival. It appears five times in the Old Testament, including passages in Ezra and Daniel. Its basic function is to express someone or something coming into a location, situation, or scene. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains coming or arriving. This word is found only in the Hebrew Old Testament occurrences represented here.

This Hebrew noun refers to “Arcturus,” a named object in the heavens. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Job: 9:9 and 38:32. Thus, its ordinary function is to identify a particular celestial body rather than describe an action, quality, or person. The word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic reference remains the same: Arcturus.

It appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah and Lamentations, and its consistent rendering as “lamentation” points to mourning expressed openly rather than quiet sadness alone. The word functions as a noun, naming the sorrowful expression itself. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: grief voiced in lament.

This Hebrew word means “thirst,” describing a strong physical need or longing for water. It is used as a verb, expressing that someone or something is thirsty rather than naming thirst as an object. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains an intense need for water or refreshment.

e.t: Kish is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a man rather than expressing an action or quality. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding family or historical context in each passage.

This Hebrew word means “fourth,” describing the person, thing, or position that comes after the third in an ordered sequence. It is used throughout the Old Testament for ordered times, places, groups, and portions, rather than naming one particular object. The word occurs 55 times in the Hebrew Bible, from Genesis through Zechariah. Its consistent use points to a straightforward ordinal meaning: the fourth member or division in a series.

This Hebrew word means “secret”—something hidden, concealed, or not openly known. It is used in Daniel for a matter beyond ordinary human discovery, especially knowledge that must be revealed rather than figured out by human skill alone. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel, where it consistently refers to hidden knowledge or a mystery requiring disclosure. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains something concealed from human understanding until it is made known.

This Hebrew word describes joyful, triumphant expression—an outward display of gladness that may be expressed in singing. It can describe the joyful sound associated with celebration or the triumphing of the wicked, so its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs four times in the Old Testament, in Job and Psalms. Its uses include joyful expression in Job and Psalms and singing before God.

This Hebrew word functions as a preposition expressing the relation “in.” It connects a person, thing, or action with a place, setting, or circumstance. In its Old Testament occurrences, it appears thirteen times, mostly in Daniel and once in Ezra. Its precise force depends on the words around it, but its ordinary role is to mark being within or situated in something. The word is therefore a grammatical connector rather than a description of a person, object, or action by itself.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “table,” a physical piece of furniture or surface. It is used as an ordinary noun throughout the Old Testament, including descriptions connected with the tabernacle and temple furnishings, as well as other settings. The word occurs 71 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic meaning is well established rather than limited to one passage. Its precise significance in any verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the table.

“Take” is a Hebrew verb describing the action of taking something or someone. It functions as an action word, with its exact object and force determined by the sentence in which it appears. In the Old Testament, this word occurs 16 times across 12 verses, including passages in Ruth, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, and Zechariah. Its uses therefore cover a recurring action rather than a rare or specialized term. Context is needed to understand precisely what is taken in each occurrence.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “joy”—a state of gladness and cheerful delight. It can describe the happiness people experience and express, especially in shared celebration. In the Old Testament it occurs 94 times, showing that this is a well-established word for joyful experience rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its uses can connect joy with receiving good things, communal celebration, and thankful enjoyment. The precise shade depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central meaning remains joy.

This Hebrew verb expresses “change,” describing an action in which something or someone is changed. Its forms may be rendered “change” or “changed,” depending on how the sentence presents the action. The word is used across 21 Old Testament occurrences, including descriptions of doubled amounts, altered appearance, a repeated action, and a changed condition. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “heat” and functions as a noun, naming a physical condition rather than expressing an action, person, or place. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Isaiah, so its use is limited and concrete rather than broad or abstract. The word appears in Isaiah 35:7 and Isaiah 49:10. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

In Hebrew Scripture, this word expresses the idea of “equal.” It functions as a predicate, stating that a person, thing, or matter is equal in the relevant comparison. The word occurs 18 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic sense appears across several settings rather than belonging to one isolated passage. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being compared there.
